newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Mandela invite sparks talk of Timor initiative.
newsitem.headline: Mandela invite sparks talk of Timor initiative.

text.p: Nelson Mandela's invitation to East Timor Nobel laureate Jose Ramos Horta for talks sparked speculation on Thursday that the charismatic South African may take a role in the dispute over the Pacific territory.
Ramos Horta, who shared the 1996 Peace prize with Timor bishop Carlos Belo, was to travel to South Africa on Thursday night to meet Mandela on Friday at the request of the South African President.

The invitation arrived only on Wednesday, hours after news emerged that Mandela, once the world's most famous political prisoner, had met jailed Timor resistance leader Xanana Gusmao during a recent visit to Indonesia.
The former Portuguese colony of East Timor, 500 km (300 miles) northwest of Australia, was annexed by Indonesia in 1976 a year after Portugal pulled out.

Up to 200,000 people are believed to have died in the takeover and a subsequent famine. The Indonesian move has never been recognised by the United Nations which continues to regard Lisbon as the territory's legal administrator.

Gusmao, 50, who is serving 20 years for resisting Indonesian rule, was taken from Jakarta's notorious Cipinang jail for dinner with Mandela at the State Guest House adjacent to President Suharto's state palace.

The two men were joined by Indonesia's roving ambassador on East Timor Lopez Da Cruz, who described the atmosphere as "informal and friendly." Mandela subsequently said that the meeting had been at his request but he gave no further details.

While applauding Mandela's interest, Ramos Horta told journalists in Lisbon that he saw no alternative at present to pursuing United Nations-brokered contacts between Lisbon and Jakarta aimed at resolving the diplomatic tussle.
"I don't believe that we can get away from the actual approach of the United Nations," he said when asked whether something new was in the offing.
In Jakarta, Indonesian officials said that they were unaware of any new initiative being undertaken by Mandela.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has sought to give new impetus to talks between Portugal and Indonesia on East Timor.
The two countries, whose foreign ministers had been staging largely fruitless six-monthly meetings, will instead hold more frequent, lower-level contacts aimed at finding common ground.
Lisbon, for whom East Timor is a foreign policy priority, is demanding that the East Timorese be given the right to decide their future in a referendum.
Jakarta, which has thousands of soldiers stationed in the territory, counters that East Timor opted for union in a vote several years ago.
There are still periodic clashes between security forces and a small guerrilla band, numbered at some 200 by the Indonesians.
It will be the second meeting between Mandela and Ramos Horta, who is Gusmao's spokesman in exile. The two men met in Johannesburg last September shortly before the award of the Nobel prize.

Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres called Mandela's invitation a sign of "a growing commitment on the part of the international community" to find a solution to the Timor problem which has dogged relations between the European Union and Asian states.
